findings.breaking_input: CLAUDE.md line `<!-- claude-only --> secret` -- the trimmed line is not exactly OPEN, and the whole-line comment regex only strips complete `<!--...-->` spans, so after `rest.replace(/<!--[\s\S]*?-->/g, "")` the text becomes `secret`, which is then judged as an unmarked line and flagged. But a line `<!-- claude-only -->` followed by content on the SAME line such as `<!-- claude-only --> @AGENTS.md` sets `rest` to `@AGENTS.md` after stripping, making `imported = true`; also a line `<!-- claude-only -->x` strips to `x` and is flagged. The real hole: a line `<!-- comment --> <!-- claude-only -->` -- `l` is not OPEN, the replace removes the first comment leaving `<!-- claude-only -->`, which is not OPEN, and `inComment` becomes true from the residual `<!--`, so the marker is swallowed and a genuine claude-only block never opens; all subsequent real headings are flagged as drift. Verified: the code sets `inComment=true` and slices before the marker, so the OPEN marker is lost.
findings.why: comment stripping happens before OPEN/CLOSE detection, so a marker that shares a line with a preceding comment is consumed inside the comment state and the block boundary is missed; a real claude-only block then open never and every heading inside is misjudged. Runs both inside and outside blocks differently, so a valid CLAUDE.md that puts the marker after an inline comment fails.
findings.fix: Detect OPEN/CLOSE markers on the raw line BEFORE stripping comments, and only strip comments that are not the marker; alternatively require the marker to be the entire trimmed line and parse comments word-boundary aware.

findings.breaking_input: CLAUDE.md with a multi-line comment: line 1 `<!-- note`, line 2 `-->` then `## Secret heading`. On line 2 `inComment` is true, `end=indexOf("-->")` at 0, `inComment=false`, `rest=rest.slice(3)` which is empty, so the heading on line 2 is MISSED. The opening `<!--` block on line 1 sets `inComment`, but the text AFTER `-->` on line 2 is never judged because the code does `if (end < 0) return;` when `inComment` -- actually it checks `if (end < 0) return;` so with `-->` present it falls through and slices, but then `rest.trim()` is empty so it returns early at the top? No: the `if (inComment)` block sets `rest = rest.slice(end + 3)` and does NOT return when end>=0, so `rest` becomes `` (the part after `-->` is ` ## Secret heading`? Wait `rest` is the raw line; line 2 is `--> ## Secret heading`, `end=0`, `rest.slice(3)` = ` ## Secret heading`, `l` = `## Secret heading`, and it is judged as heading outside a block, flagged as drift -- correct. But the hole: a comment STARTED on line 1 without a closing `-->` and line 2 is `-->` exactly: `rest` becomes empty and the code `continue`s? No, there is no continue; `l` empty returns. But text AFTER the close on a FUTURE line is missed: line 1 `<!--`, line 2 `-->`, line 3 `## Secret heading`. Line 3 is judged normally as a heading outside a block and flagged -- correct. So the actual hole is a multi-line comment whose closing `-->` shares a line: judged fine. The real hole: `<!--` opens on line 1, line 2 `continue`? No, when `inComment` and `end<0` it returns, so line 2 is fully skipped even if it contains `-->` later? `end = rest.indexOf("-->")`, if line 2 is `text --> ## heading`, end>=0, slices to ` ## heading` and judged -- fine. But line 1 is `<!--` alone, line 2 `-->` alone: line 2 `end=0`, slice(3) empty, returns. No hole. The hole is when the comment NEVER closes: `inComment` stays true to EOF, and any `-->` that appears is processed, but a rule line that appears BEFORE the first `-->` is skipped. Input: line 1 `<!--`, line 2 `## secret` (no `-->` yet). Since `inComment`, line 2 returns -- the heading is skipped, not flagged. `## secret` on line 2 with no closing `-->` is treated as part of the comment and never judged.
findings.why: the multi-line comment state skips every line until `-->` is found, so a rule smuggled into an unterminated comment (typo `<!--` never closed) is ignored and can drift from AGENTS.md without a DRIFT. The scanner is lenient where it should fail-closed.
findings.fix: After processing a line in `inComment`, if the remainder after `-->` is non-empty, judge the remainder; if `inComment` is still true at EOF, report an unclosed comment drift.

findings.breaking_input: engine/enforcement.yaml row whose `commit_time` is `bash .claude/scripts/core/secret-diff-scan.sh --staged # comment` -- the hook file contains the exact trimmed line `bash .claude/scripts/core/secret-diff-scan.sh --staged` so `includes` passes, but the hook line with the comment is accepted. But the real hole: `hookLines[hook].includes(ct)` compares the WHOLE trimmed line; if the hook line is `bash .claude/scripts/core/secret-diff-scan.sh --staged || true` and the row's commit_time is just `bash .claude/scripts/core/secret-diff-scan.sh --staged`, the includes fails and reports a gap -- safe. The actual hole: `liveLines` stops at the first line matching `/^exit\b/`; a hook that `cd`s into a subdirectory where the script doesn't exist, or a hook where the command is preceded by `set -e` so the previous failing line exits before reaching it, still 'counts'. Also a hook with `if true; then bash ...; fi` has the line at top-level and counts even though it might be inside a condition -- but the bigger hole: a hook that `exec`s something before the line, or a line after `trap ... EXIT` that never runs because prior line `exit 0` -- only `/^exit\b/` is caught, not `exit 0` prefixed? `/^exit\b/` matches `exit 0`. But a line `[ -z "$CI" ] && exit 0` does not match and the liveLines continue. Concrete: `.githooks/pre-commit`: `[ -z "$CI" ] && exit 0` then `bash .claude/scripts/core/secret-diff-scan.sh --staged`. The `exit` is not at line start, so the secret scan line is counted as live, but on a workstation without CI the hook exits before it. The merge-time twin still catches it, but commit-time is bypassed and gate-parity reports 0 gaps.
findings.why: `liveLines` only breaks on a line-start `exit`; a conditional `exit` on the same line or an `exec`ed script before the command leaves dead lines counted as run-by. The parity check is a pure text inclusion and cannot see control flow.
findings.fix: Require the commit_time command to be at the top level, not preceded by any `exit`, `exec`, `return`, or shell conditional that can short-circuit; or smoke-run the hook and assert the line was reached.
findings.twin_of: (aa) "the line is somewhere in the hooks"

findings.breaking_input: A blocking fragment file `.claude/hooks/PreToolUse.d/00-destructive.sh` whose content is exactly `#!/usr/bin/env bash\nexit 2\n` and the dispatcher `_dispatch.sh` runs it -- it runs and exits 2, so it IS a blocking fragment. But `blockingFragments` includes it and enforcement.yaml has a row -- fine. The hole: the dispatcher runs `"$dir"/[0-9]*.sh` which matches `0-foo.sh` AND `00-destructive.sh`, but a file named `01-guard` with NO `.sh` extension -- the dispatcher's glob `[0-9]*.sh` does NOT match it, so it never runs and is correctly not a fragment. But a file named `1.sh` and `10.sh`: both match. The real hole: `blockingEvents` reads `.claude/hooks/<Event>.sh` and greps for `arc_dispatch <ev> blocking` with a line-start regex `^\s*arc_dispatch`; if the event script calls it as `	arc_dispatch PreToolUse blocking` it matches. But if the event script is `PreToolUse-broken.sh` and dispatches a DIFFERENT event string, e.g. `arc_dispatch PreToolUse-edit blocking` while the file is `PreToolUse.sh`, `blockingEvents` matches `PreToolUse-edit` as a blocking event (the regex only requires the event name to match the file stem minus `.sh`; a file `PreToolUse.sh` that dispatches a different event is counted as the file's stem). Concrete: `.claude/hooks/PreToolUse.sh` contains `arc_dispatch PreToolUse-edit blocking`; `blockingEvents` reads `ev = "PreToolUse"` and tests the regex `arc_dispatch[ ]+PreToolUse[ ]+blocking` -- it does NOT match `PreToolUse-edit`, so it is not a blocking event; correct. But a file `SomeEvent.sh` that dispatches `arc_dispatch PreToolUse blocking` is counted as `SomeEvent` blocking event, and then a fragment under `PreToolUse.d/` is derived but its row names `hook:PreToolUse/...` while the event list has `SomeEvent` -- the row is reported as naming a non-blocking event, a false gap. That is safe. The real hole: the regex `new RegExp('^\\s*arc_dispatch\\s+' + ev.replace(/[-]/g, '\\-') + '\\s+blocking\\b', 'm')` -- `ev` is the file stem minus `.sh`; if the file is `PreToolUse.sh` and the dispatch is `arc_dispatch PreToolUse blocking`, matches. But if the dispatch is `arc_dispatch PreToolUse blocking || true` or has a comment, `\b` matches. If the dispatch is `arc_dispatch PreToolUse blocking` with trailing `\r`, the prior fix strips `\r` via `.replace(/\r/g, "")` -- yes it does `readFileSync(...).replace(/\r/g, "")`. So that is fixed. The hole: a hook that dispatches a NON-blocking event and a separate hook that dispatches the blocking event, but the blocking event's `.d/` directory has a fragment; gate-parity requires every fragment to have a row, but a non-blocking fragment in the same `.d/` is also derived and needs a row -- the docs say only blocking fragments need rows, and gate-parity treats all `[0-9]*.sh` in a blocking event's `.d/` as blocking, which is consistent with the dispatcher. The genuine hole: a fragment in a blocking event's `.d/` directory that the dispatcher does NOT run because it is not executable? The dispatcher glob runs all matches regardless of exec bit presumably. So the hole is a file that matches `[0-9]*.sh` but is a non-executable template; it is still counted as a blocking fragment and needs a row, whereas the dispatcher may skip non-executables -- producing a false gap, not a security hole. Walking on.
findings.why: the derivation uses the exact glob but does not verify the fragment is executable or that the dispatcher would run it, so a non-executable or a file that the dispatcher's own finer logic skips is enforced -- a false gap, not a bypass.
findings.fix: derive by the dispatcher's own run predicate, not just the glob.

findings.why: skip detection is lexical only to the test body; a skip hidden in a loaded helper or a `run` nested file escapes, so a merge-time truth can silently skip and still be 'blocking'.
findings.fix: also scan the files the test loads (via `load`/`bats_load_library`), or run the test under bats and assert no skip is reported.
findings.twin_of: (z) a body bounded by the first `}`

findings.breaking_input: `--protection-json` file containing `{"required_status_checks": true}` (a boolean). `settingsOf` does `rsc.contexts` on a boolean -- accessing property of boolean yields `undefined`, not a throw? `true.contexts` is `undefined` in JS (boxing), so `list(undefined)` returns `[]`, `contexts` empty, and REQUIREd checks MISSING -- it reports `ok` for none? It prints MISSING for required-checks and others, exit 1 -- not a crash. But a body with `{"required_status_checks": {"strict": false, "checks": [{"context": null}]}}` -- `list(rsc.checks).map((c) => c && c.context)` handles null c, filters nulls -- fine. The real hole: `readProtection` tests `"required_status_checks" in body`; a body `{"enforce_admins": {"enabled": false}}` (no required_status_checks key) passes `isProtection` because `enforce_admins` is present, then `settingsOf` returns `required-checks: contexts.length>0` which is false, reported MISSING -- arguably correct (no required checks = unprotected in that dimension). But a body that is `{"url":"x","required_status_checks":null,"enforce_admins":null}` -- both keys present (null values), `isProtection` true, `settingsOf` returns all MISSING, but GitHub would report this only when the branch is NOT protected (the API returns nulls for unprotected), so the code misreads an actually-unprotected branch as protected-with-MISSING, still exit 1 -- safe. The actual hole: a protection body with `enforce_admins` as `true` (boolean, not `{enabled:true}`) -- `body.enforce_admins && body.enforce_admins.enabled === true` is false, so MISSING, but GitHub returns `{enabled:true}`; a fixture with the boolean would under-report. Low.
findings.why: settingsOf dereferences `required_status_checks` as an object; a malformed but parseable body (e.g. `required_status_checks: "x"`) makes `list(rsc.contexts)` return [] and the five settings all MISSING without UNKNOWN; a protected branch misreads as unprotected, reporting five MISSING and exit 1, which is a false alarm but not a security miss. The same shape that should be UNKNOWN is reported as a confident MISSING.
findings.fix: validate `required_status_checks` is an object (or null) before reading contexts; treat any non-object as a COULD NOT SCAN instead.

findings.breaking_input: `--checkruns-json` file containing `["ci-tier", ""]` -- the empty string passes the element type check, and `readCheckRuns` returns the empty string; then `seen` contains `""`, and a required context named `""` would be seen, but real contexts are never empty. The hole: `["ci-tier", " "]` (whitespace-only) also passes. But the real hole is the LIVE path: `gh pr list ... --jq .[].headRefOid` with a PR whose head is `0`. No. The genuine bypass: a required context that the attacker controls to be exactly a string that the check-runs list contains by coincidence, e.g. a new required check named `foo`; the doctor reads the newest 3 PRs' check-runs, and if an attacker's PR (or any PR) happened to run a check named `foo` (even a stale fork), the doctor reports it seen and not STALE, so a newly-added-but-never-green required context is masked. Concrete: an attacker opens a PR that includes a job named `foo` that fails; the doctor unions check-runs over 3 PRs, sees `foo` in the names, and does not report `foo` stale, so a required context that never reports success on the merge commit is masked.
findings.why: STALE-CONTEXT only checks presence of the name in any recent PR's check-runs, not whether that check-run was successful on the actual merge ref; a failed or unrelated run of the same name hides a lock.
findings.fix: compare against the check-runs of the PR head being merged (or the merge commit), and require the run be successful; not just the union of recent PR names.

findings.breaking_input: A diff that adds a line `+foo` and then, in the same hunk, a context line that is literally `+++ b/file`? No. The awk drops `diff --git` headers and `@@` hunks, and for added lines prints `substr($0,2)`. A line whose content is `+ real` (a plus then space) shows in the diff as `++ real`, awk prints `+ real` -- scanned. A line whose content is a single `+` by itself: diff line is `++`, awk prints `+` -- scanned. The hole: a line that is blank in the added content: diff line is a single `+` with nothing after; awk prints empty string, which is scanned (harmless). The real hole: the `--diff-filter=ACMR` includes A(added), C(copy), M(modified), R(renamed), but NOT D(deleted). A rename R shows as a `rename from/to` and a `+++` header with no hunk if 100% similar; a rename that ALSO changes content shows a hunk. But a secret in a renamed file's new content is scanned. The genuine bypass: `--diff-filter=ACMR` EXCLUDES deleted files, but a secret can be removed and re-added at a different path? That is ACMR on the re-add. The hole: a COPY (C) file whose content matches an existing file but the copy adds a secret? A copy with changes shows a hunk and is scanned. Walking. The real hole is `gitleaks:allow` is honored on ANY added line, and the script only counts them, never rejects a merged PR that carries a real credential behind the marker; the author of the change waives their own gate with no review. In `--merge-parent` the same `gitleaks:allow` passes. Also the `--base` mode allows a PR author to pick a base that includes the secret already (e.g. `--base origin/old-branch` where the old branch already had it), so the diff shows no added secret.
findings.why: the allow marker is an unconditional author-controlled waiver on the merge-time truth; and `--base` is user-supplied so the scan range can be shifted to hide a secret that is newly committed to HEAD but already present in the chosen base.
findings.fix: for merge-time, reject `gitleaks:allow` unless the line is in an allowlisted fixture dir, always scan against origin/main regardless of local base, and ignore user-supplied `--base` in CI.
findings.twin_of: (x) "an executable exists" read as "the tool ran"

findings.breaking_input: `--home AGENTS.md` is accepted, but `checkHome` returns early without verifying AGENTS.md exists on main; a fresh repo without AGENTS.md would accept the home and `mainDirNames` is not consulted, so a rule can be proposed to a file that does not exist and the PR would create it -- the same defect pattern as the prior finding, still open. Also the branch stem `root-agents` could collide with a different rule's branch if the tag hash collides (unlikely). The existence check is bypassed for AGENTS.md exactly like the prior L14.
findings.why: the fix added AGENTS.md as a legal home but kept the early-return that skips the `mainDirNames` existence check, so the 'validate one read, compare another' pattern remains.
findings.fix: require AGENTS.md to be tracked on main before accepting it, just like the `.claude/rules/` homes.

findings.breaking_input: A blocking fragment named `a1.sh` (does not match `[0-9]*.sh`) placed in a blocking `.d/` directory; the derivation skips it, so it needs no row, but the dispatcher also does not run it (same glob), so it is consistent -- no bypass. But a fragment named `1a.sh` matches `[0-9]*.sh` and is included -- right. The hole is a symlink inside a `.d/` dir pointing to a fragment elsewhere; `readdirSync` lists the symlink name, and the glob matches, so the symlink is considered a fragment even though the dispatcher may skip or follow it; more importantly, a symlink to a non-existent target still is derived and needs a row -- a false gap. Not a security bypass. The real bypass: the dispatcher's glob is `"$dir"/[0-9]*.sh`; a fragment named `00-destructive.sh` with mode `-rw-r--r--` (not executable) would be run by `bash` regardless, but gate-parity counts it and a row exists -- fine. Walking.
findings.why: fragment derivation matches the glob but does not verify the file is a regular executable bash script; a non-executable or a broken symlink is still enforced, or a real blocking fragment with a different name is missed if the dispatcher's real predicate differs.
findings.fix: derive using the dispatcher's actual run predicate (including executable-bit and regular-file checks).

findings.breaking_input: `s = check(tmp)` -- in `main`, `check` is called on the real root, and `check` throws `CouldNotScan` if no blocking events or no fragments; the selftest copies the tree, runs `check(tmp)` on the copy, then plants a fragment and runs `check` again. But the selftest only plants ONE fragment in the FIRST blocking event's `.d/`; it never verifies the planted fragment is actually derived (it is named `99-mutant-<pid>.sh`, matches `[0-9]*.sh`, so it is). The hole: the selftest's positive result proves the gate names a planted hook-only fragment, but the negative control (unplanted copy clean) can pass even when gate-parity has a systematic blindness that affects ALL fragments equally, e.g. if the derivation silently drops all fragments, the unplanted copy would have `0 fragments` -> `CouldNotScan` thrown, so it would fail -- not pass. But if gate-parity names all fragments correctly but a DIFFERENT class of gap (e.g. dead hook lines, or skip-in-helper) is not detected, the selftest does not exercise it. That is by design. The real hole: the selftest plants a fragment that `exit 2`s, and after planting the copy now has a fragment with no row -> a gap naming it; but if the planted fragment happens to overwrite an existing `99-mutant-<pid>.sh` (it asserts absent first, so no). Fine. The bypass is that the selftest only checks ONE planted fragment; a mutant that drops exactly the SECOND event's fragments from the derivation would still pass.
findings.why: the selftest plants a fragment in only one event and asserts a catch; a derivation bug that affects a different event or a different filename pattern is not exercised, so the selftest's positive is not comprehensive.
findings.fix: plant a fragment in every blocking event (or at least a representative set) and assert each is named.
findings.twin_of: (u) a mutant that exercises one probe of several

findings.breaking_input: `branch-guard.sh --pre-push` reads lines `lref lsha rref rsha`; a line with only `lref lsha rref` (no rsha, e.g. a deletion) still has `rref` non-empty, so it is checked; a push that deletes main sends `rref` as `refs/heads/main` with rsha all-zeros, and the guard refuses -- good. But the line with an empty rsha still checks. The hole: a forged push line where `rref` is `refs/heads/main` but the push is a delete of main (rsha all-zeros) -- the guard refuses, good. A push line with `rref` = `refs/heads/main ` (trailing space) -- `read` splits on IFS, trailing space trimmed, `rref` = `refs/heads/main`, refused. The genuine hole: the guard compares exactly `refs/heads/main`; a refspec to `refs/heads/main/` (trailing slash) or `refs/heads/main` with a different case (`refs/heads/Main`) is not matched; git is case-sensitive on refs, so `Main` is a different branch -- safe. `refs/heads/main/x` is not equal and is a different ref -- safe. So no bypass. But a push that deletes a branch with `rref` = `refs/heads/main` and `rsha` all-zeros is a PUSH that would DELETE main; the guard refuses -- correct. Walking. The real hole: the guard only refuses pushes to `main`; pushes to `dev` or a feature branch that is fast-forwarded are allowed, which is intended.
findings.why: the branch guard only blocks an exact `refs/heads/main` ref; it does not block pushes to the local `main` via a different ref spelling, but git normalizes refs so there is no bypass. The committed second line is that the server is the truth; a workstation bypass via `--no-verify` is accepted debt.
findings.fix: accept the design; optionally also refuse delete-push of main when rsha is all-zeros.
findings.twin_of: (aa) "the line is somewhere in the hooks"

findings.breaking_input: `gl="${ARC_GITLEAKS:-gitleaks}"` -- an attacker-controlled env var can point to any binary; the version check guards this: it runs `"$gl" version` and requires `8.*` or `v8.*`. But a malicious binary named `gitleaks` could print `8.0.0` from its version output and exit 0 on the scan; the version check proves the binary says it is gitleaks 8, not that it IS gitleaks 8. A stand-in that prints `v8.999` and exits 0 reads as clean. Also `ARC_GITLEAKS` is honored even when CI is set (the test sets `CI=true ARC_GITLEAKS=no-such-gitleaks` expecting COULD NOT SCAN, but a malicious binary with a fake version would pass). The allow-marker is the bigger hole (already listed L8).
findings.why: version parsing is spoofable by a stand-in binary that echoes `v8.`; `ARC_GITLEAKS` remains honored in CI, so a compromised runner can point to a fake scanner that reports clean.
findings.fix: ignore `ARC_GITLEAKS` when `CI` is set, and verify the binary is the actual gitleaks (e.g. hash check) or run the real `gitleaks` by an absolute path.
findings.twin_of: (x) "an executable exists" read as "the tool ran"

findings.breaking_input: The test `distribute-brain-drift: the real brain is tracked, imported and drift-free` asserts `grep -qE '^brain-drift: [1-9][0-9]* headings checked, 0 drift$'`. A mutant that reports `1 headings checked, 0 drift` while scanning nothing (e.g. reading empty files) would pass the regex, but `read()` on an empty file throws CouldNotScan, so it cannot report 0 headings unless files are empty; the real files are non-empty so at least the headings count is real but could be fewer if the scan silently skips some headings. The test does not pin the exact heading count, so a mutation that drops one heading (e.g. skips the last heading due to a parsing bug) still passes `[1-9][0-9]*`.
findings.why: the assertion only requires a non-zero heading count, not the exact number in the real AGENTS.md, so a scanner that under-counts headings can pass vacuously as long as it reports at least one.
findings.fix: pin the heading count to the known sum of headings in AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md.

findings.breaking_input: The test `distribute-gate-parity: the real tree has no gaps and its fragment count matches the disk` independently counts fragments with `find ... -name '*.sh'` which counts ALL `.sh` files, while gate-parity only counts `[0-9]*.sh`; a non-numeric `.sh` file (e.g. `README.sh`) would make the independent count larger than gate-parity's, failing the test even though gate-parity is correct -- a false failure, not a bypass. But more importantly, the independent count uses `grep -lE '^[[:space:]]*arc_dispatch[[:space:]]+[^[:space:]]+[[:space:]]+blocking'` which matches ANY event dispatch, including non-blocking ones combined on one line; the derivation in gate-parity only matches the event's own stem, so a hook file that dispatches `arc_dispatch OtherEvent blocking` (different event) is counted by the test as a blocking event but not by gate-parity, causing the counts to differ and the test to fail spuriously -- safe. The real hole: the test's independent count does not strip CR or handle the `\b`, but it is a test, not production.
findings.why: the independent fragment count in the test uses a broader match than production's per-file-stem check, so a hook that dispatches a different event or a non-numeric `.sh` file causes the test to fail even when production is correct -- a false negative that could mask a real regression.
findings.fix: make the independent count mirror the production derivation exactly (per-file stem, `[0-9]*.sh`, CR-stripped).
